avatars.name: The Late Starter
avatars.tagline: A man who never really got going with dating and now feels behind everyone he knows.
avatars.who: A single man, usually late 20s to early 40s (with an older tail in his 50s), who has never had an official girlfriend or whose longest relationship lasted a few months. He gets few or no matches, ends up in the friend zone, or gets first dates that never turn into second ones, and he freezes or overthinks around women he likes. Many work hands-on or hourly jobs, live in small towns or rural areas, and are in therapy for anxiety, depression or old family wounds. He books the call because he has run out of ideas on his own and wants someone to show him, step by step, what he is doing wrong.

profile.relationship_history: Never had a committed relationship, or only short flings and 'almosts'. Some were burned once (cheated on, an abusive partner, a one-sided friendship) and have been single for years since.
profile.work_and_money: Mixed and often thin: tradesmen, techs, hospitality, freelancers, people between jobs or with no income, plus a few salaried IT or office workers. Money is the most common blocker; several had no savings, no credit or under a thousand dollars available.
profile.apps_and_tried: Hinge, Tinder or Facebook Dating with few or no replies; some have stopped using apps. Tried therapy, books, YouTube or pickup content, friends reviewing profiles, speed dating, and in a couple of cases a previous dating coach that did not help.

goals: A first real, committed relationship that leads to marriage and kids
Confidence to start conversations and approach women without freezing
An honest outside read, ideally from a woman, on what he is doing wrong
Move from first dates and friend zone to a second date and real interest
Stop feeling behind his friends and family
Someone to come home to instead of evenings alone
pains: Few or no matches, and women go quiet once he asks them out
Stuck in the friend zone or first dates that fizzle with no explanation
Anxiety, overthinking and freezing around women he is attracted to
Low self-worth: feels like a loser, not marriage material, or too late
Lonely evenings and few places to meet women, especially in small towns
Embarrassment at family events and watching friends get married

objections.quote: $7,200 is a lot. The money is stretched thin at the moment.

objections.quote: at $7,200 for three months, that's over $2,000 a month. And if I only meet with her four times a month, that's what, $400 or $500 a session? So that's a lot.

objections.what_it_really_means: He has been told yes and then let down before, so he needs time away from pressure to trust his own decision.
objections.quote: I don't want to sign or pay anything today. I want to have a little bit of time to think over this first.

objections.what_it_really_means: Money is fine; the fear is paying for a second coach who also gives generic advice and no result.

The program covers that well (Reset, Inner Game, Read and Lead), but at $7,200 it is priced above what many of these men can pay, so the bi-weekly $3,600 tier is the realistic fit and should be the recommendation when money is tight.

avatars.name: The Rusty Returner
avatars.tagline: A divorced or widowed man in his 50s or 60s who was good at this once and now feels lost on the apps.
avatars.who: An older man, usually divorced (sometimes widowed or grieving), who has been out of the dating world for years or has drifted from one wrong relationship to the next. He is often successful or comfortable (business owner, lawyer, pilot, tech) but some are on pensions, two jobs or fixed incomes. The apps feel like a minefield of fakes, scams and flakes, he gets few replies or one date that goes nowhere, and he worries about seeming too old or creepy. He is on the call because he is lonely, the clock feels real, and he wants a guide for a game whose rules changed.

profile.age: 41 to 72, most in their mid 50s to 60s
profile.relationship_history: Long marriage ended in divorce (or a spouse died), then years of little or no dating, or a string of on-and-off relationships with women who were not a match or wanted money.
profile.work_and_money: Split. Some are secure (retired business owners, lawyers, Google, pilots) and the money is not the issue; others are on pensions, fixed incomes or rebuilding after a failed business and are heavily price-anchored.
profile.kids: Often grown or teenage kids; a few still raising young children after divorce.
profile.apps_and_tried: Match, Tinder, Facebook Dating, eHarmony, Christian Mingle, Hinge. Many have already paid for matchmaking or another coach (including in-person or pickup-style coaches) and feel it did not deliver.

goals: A long-term partner for the next 20 or 30 years, someone who has his back
Get his confidence and old self back with women
Know where to meet the right women offline and which apps to use
Read women's intentions early and spot fakes, scams and gold-diggers
A better profile, photos and messages that actually get replies
Companionship: travel, dinners, someone beside him at the end of the day
pains: Apps full of fake profiles, bots, scams and women who will not meet
Few replies or one date that never becomes a second
Loneliness and the fear of dying alone
Feels too old, worries about seeming creepy or being written off
Keeps choosing or attracting the wrong women
Already paid for matchmaking or coaching that did not work

Career took priority for years, friends are now getting married, and he has started to feel the clock. He books the call because he is self-aware, often in therapy, and wants a practical outside read on why nothing becomes official.

profile.work_and_money: Salaried professionals or business heirs who can usually invest four figures, though some cap what they will spend on 'help they don't really need'.

avatars.name: The Clock-Watcher

She is on the call because she has done the therapy and the reading and wants practical, directive dating guidance.

profile.kids: Mostly no kids; many want one soon.

avatars.who_buys: Buyers name a repeating pattern in their own words, have the money or credit to act on the call, and decide alone: professional women around 40 with an unavailable-men or long situationship pattern, men around 30 with good careers whose relationships never become official, a wealthy older divorced man, and younger novices who came warm from Kim's content. They hit a high score on the temperature check before price and their only objection is which tier or how to pay. Non-buyers mostly fall into three groups: people who cannot invest four figures (no income, fixed income, debt, or a few hundred dollars), people who want a single session or a verdict on one person rather than a program, and older sceptics who were burned by a past coach or matchmaker and ask for guarantees. Across all groups the calls that were lost usually had price stated before money was qualified, and then improvised discounts, deposits and financing pushes.
avatars.icp_gap: The closing doc describes four segments split evenly by gender, with the successful woman as the achiever and an older divorced woman as the rebuilder. In practice the ad funnel targets men and its applicants skew 55 and over, so most sales calls are with men, many of them older returners on mixed incomes or late-starting novices with little money. A large share of calls fall outside the four segments: men around 30 who date easily but cannot make it official, and people who only want help with one specific person. The people who actually buy are professional women in their late 30s and 40s and men in their 30s with careers, plus the occasional wealthy older man; older women and one-situation callers rarely buy. The sanctioned $3,600 bi-weekly tier matches what many novices and older women can pay, yet it is seldom offered and reps invent cheaper options instead.

scripts.summary: Reps run the discovery half well (why now on 90% of calls, doubt question 81%, pillars 64 to 81%) but the back half is improvised: money is never qualified before the pitch (0 of 55 calls), 26 of 47 pitched calls quoted an off-sheet price (the $1,000 first session on 15, the $2,400 starter on 9), 37 of 55 carried an outcome promise such as '80% find a partner', and next steps before price were run in full on 6 of 47. The three changes that matter most: lock prices to $3,600 / $7,200 / $14,000 with Tier 1.5 as the planned lower option, add a budget check before the pitch, and add the missing safety sections (recording disclosure, crisis pause, prospect-only financing applications). Nov 17 edit: no change is detectable. playbook_closer.json already cites the 2026-11-17 edit and was written at 01:25 UTC on 18 Nov, after the 19:19 UTC edit; every one of its 51 checks and 3 prices matches the current text, and Drive returned no revision history. Text in the current doc that the playbook does not score: the 'when did you realize / specific event' probes, 'How long has it been like this for you?' in Current Situation, the optional proof point in Transition, the pillar working-names note, and the 'Tier 2/3' delivery line. All 55 analysed calls (5 Jun to 11 Nov) predate the edit, so the patches target the current text.

patches.reality: 26 of 47 pitched calls (55%) quoted at least one price that is not on the sheet, 15 distinct prices in all. The two that recur: a $1,000 'first call / first session with Kim' on 15 calls and a $2,400 '6 weeks, 4 sessions' or 'first month' starter on 9 calls. Also $13,900 and $13,997 for the $14,000 tier, $3,400, $3,500, $3,800 and $4,000 for the $3,600 tier, and $500 or $337 entries. Calls with an off-sheet price closed 2 of 26 (8%); pitched calls that stayed on the sheet closed 5 of 21 (24%). The $1,000 offer turned into a $100 deposit on one call and a 'Foundation Program' at $2,400 in the CRM on another.

Where the prospect asked to pay for one session first (recQgbOLAOMtxKfce), the close came from a 1 to 10 check and a payment split, not a new product.
patches.change: Add a hard rule under TIER MAPPING: the only prices a closer says are $3,600, $7,200 and $14,000. No trial calls, deposits for a single session, 6-week starters, first-month options or rounded numbers. If a prospect asks to try one session first, use the trial-request lines below. Anything else goes to Mitch before it is said on a call.

What the three months does is give you the first few weeks to feel the difference. What would you need to see in those first weeks to know it's working?"

patches.reality: 37 of 55 calls (67%) carried an outcome promise, with 40 outcome-promise flags. 28 calls cite a success rate: '80% find a partner in the first year' or '50% within six months and 78% within 12 months', said in near-identical words by different reps. 13 calls promise 'at least two dates a week'. Others say '100%' or 'she's going to help you find your person'. The note in the script has no approved line to replace these, so reps use the stats. Promises did not lift the close rate: 5 of 37 calls with a promise closed (14%) against 2 of 18 without.

scripts.summary: Setters follow the opening and core discovery (intro, anchor to the opt-in, biggest problem and dig-in run on 78 to 92% of calls) but the back half breaks: 16 of 18 price mentions were off the 'low to mid four figures' anchor, the money answer is weak or missing on 22 of 28 calls, and no booking had the invite accepted live. The three changes: one true price anchor said word for word, drop the credit-score DQ for a yes/no financing question, and add invite-accepted-live plus a Zoom check and a word to reschedule. All 28 recorded setter calls (9 Sep to 16 Nov) predate the 17 Nov edit. No change is detectable against playbook_setter.json, which was built after the edit and already encodes the 650 credit rule and the low-to-mid anchor.

patches.script_says: It depends entirely on the plan you come up with with our advisor, how many sessions you end up having with Kim, the timeline, etc … but for most people it ends up being in the low to mid four figure range

Only 2 used 'low to mid' or 'mid four figures'. The drift has a cause: the anchor does not match the offer ($3,600, $7,200, $14,000), and a texted lead who heard 'low to mid four figures' said he would not have taken the call had he known it was $7,200. Of 10 CRM bookings from these calls, 4 showed and 0 closed.
patches.what_works: Texts sent from the scripts used the anchor word for word (12 threads), so the wording is not the problem; the mismatch with the real prices is.
patches.change: Mitch picks one anchor that is true for the offer and every setter script uses it word for word. Until then, setters use the current line exactly and never give a dollar figure, a 'five to nine' range or a per-session price. Suggested anchor if Mitch approves: 'starts in the mid four figures'.
new_lines: It depends on how much one-on-one time with Kim makes sense for you, but most people invest somewhere in the low to mid four figures. I'm not asking you to commit to anything today. If it's the right fit, is that something that would be feasible for you?

[If they ask for an exact number] The advisor will map that out with you, because it depends on how often you'd be working with Kim. What I can tell you is it's a four-figure investment, so I just want to make sure that's realistic before we book.
[Never say] 'mid to high four figures', a dollar range like 'five to nine thousand', or a price for a single session.

scripts.script: Kimberly Rae Chapman Phone Setting Script
scripts.summary: An unfilled template written for women, while 26 of 28 recorded setter calls are with men; [RANGE] and other brackets are blank, so setters improvise price ranges. decisions_for_mitch: Approved prices: confirm the only three prices are $3,600 (3 months, bi-weekly), $7,200 (3 months, weekly) and $14,000 (6 months, weekly), and whether any entry option (a paid first session, a deposit) is allowed. Today reps invent them: $1,000 first session on 15 calls, $2,400 starter on 9.

Setter price anchor: 'low to mid four figures' does not match $7,200 or $14,000, and setters drift to 'mid to high' or '5 to 9 thousand' on 16 of 18 calls. Pick one true anchor for every setter and DM script.
Success-rate claims: the '50% within six months, 78% within 12 months' and '80% find a partner' lines are said on 28 calls. Either document them with a real source or ban them.
Recording and retention: what happens to recordings of prospects who do not buy, so the closer's disclosure line can be accurate. Reps have promised deletion on 3 calls.

Financing: which partners are approved, the rule that prospects apply on their own device with no rep hearing an SSN or income, and whether setters ever ask about credit at all (the Master Setting Doc's 650 DQ).

Crisis protocol: who gets the same-day escalation when a prospect mentions self-harm, overdose or abuse, and whether those leads are paused from sales. One texted overdose disclosure was still awaiting a human follow-up when the data was pulled (lead_nGKEZvUvxDh4ID4ImwwMm9kjJY8TVxwjo55iuDi83qM).
Approved proof points: 2 to 4 anonymous client stories per segment, with consent, so reps stop naming clients or quoting their health details.
Phone Setting Script: fill and de-gender it, or retire it and move its book-and-confirm, lock-the-show and objection-bank sections into the Master Setting Doc.

marketing.who_buys: Buyers name a repeating pattern in their own words, have the money or credit to act on the call, and decide alone: professional women around 40 with an unavailable-men or long situationship pattern, men around 30 with good careers whose relationships never become official, a wealthy older divorced man, and younger novices who came warm from Kim's content. They hit a high score on the temperature check before price and their only objection is which tier or how to pay. Non-buyers mostly fall into three groups: people who cannot invest four figures (no income, fixed income, debt, or a few hundred dollars), people who want a single session or a verdict on one person rather than a program, and older sceptics who were burned by a past coach or matchmaker and ask for guarantees. Across all groups the calls that were lost usually had price stated before money was qualified, and then improvised discounts, deposits and financing pushes.
marketing.icp_gap: The closing doc describes four segments split evenly by gender, with the successful woman as the achiever and an older divorced woman as the rebuilder. In practice the ad funnel targets men and its applicants skew 55 and over, so most sales calls are with men, many of them older returners on mixed incomes or late-starting novices with little money. A large share of calls fall outside the four segments: men around 30 who date easily but cannot make it official, and people who only want help with one specific person. The people who actually buy are professional women in their late 30s and 40s and men in their 30s with careers, plus the occasional wealthy older man; older women and one-situation callers rarely buy. The sanctioned $3,600 bi-weekly tier matches what many novices and older women can pay, yet it is seldom offered and reps invent cheaper options instead.

rubric.markdown:
# AI call review rubric: Kimberly Rae Coaching: Master Closing Doc

Use on every recorded sales call and triage call. Score each check hit / partial / miss / not applicable, quote the evidence, and post the summary to Slack within an hour of the call.

## Hard flags (any one sends the call to a manager the same day)

- **Outcome promise**: Any guarantee or implied promise that the prospect will find a partner or save the relationship, including success-rate figures not in the script.
- **Off-sheet price**: Any price, discount, trial or payment structure not on the sanctioned price sheet: $3,600 bi-weekly 1:1 with Kim; $7,200 weekly 1:1 with Kim; $14,000 weekly 1:1 with Kim.
- **Credit or ID handling**: Rep asks for, hears read aloud, or types an SSN, date of birth or income figure, or suggests what to enter on a financing application.
- **Crisis not handled**: Prospect discloses self-harm, suicidal thoughts, abuse, violence or acute crisis and the rep keeps selling without care, a crisis line or a manager note.
- **No recording disclosure**: The rep doesn't say the call is recorded in the first minutes.
- **Pressure after a clear no**: The rep keeps pushing, shames, or invents urgency after the prospect clearly declines.
- **Therapy or credential claims**: Rep implies therapy, treatment, insurance coverage or a licence, or leaves the prospect believing so.

## Sales call: Kimberly Rae Coaching: Master Closing Doc

Score = weighted share of applicable steps (hit 1, partial 0.5, miss 0).

### C1 Intro & frame (weight 10)
- C1a: States the call is confidential
- C1b: Discloses the call is recorded
- C1c: Credibility: has taken hundreds of these calls
- C1d: Invites full transparency
- C1e: Frames the goal of the call and gets agreement
- C1f: References setter notes (or Kim's DM notes) so they feel seen
- C1g: Opens with why they took an hour out of their day

### C2 Isolate the problem (weight 15)
- C2a: Asks the biggest thing not working in dating/relationships
- C2b: Asks what they mean, in their own words
- C2c: Asks if anything else is getting in the way
- C2d: Probes duration (how long, always been this way)
- C2e: Probes spillover into other areas of life

### C3 Background & segment read (weight 10)
- C3a: Relationship status (single, seeing someone, undefined)
- C3b: Apps usage
- C3c: Work and meeting people organically
- C3d: How long actively dating
- C3e: Flexes the call to the segment (novice, achiever, rebuilder, returner)

### C4 Current situation & what they've tried (weight 10)
- C4a: Gets weekly mechanics (apps time, conversations, dates)
- C4b: Asks where it usually falls apart
- C4c: Asks what they have tried (apps, coaching, books, therapy)
- C4d: Asks how that went

### C5 Doubt question (weight 10)
- C5a: Asks what they think has been getting in the way
- C5b: Does not correct the belief yet (saves it for the pitch)

### C6 Why now & cost (weight 20)
- C6a: Asks why now vs six months ago
- C6b: Asks what it has been costing them, beyond dating
- C6c: Goes deeper with a segment-aware cost question
- C6d: Magic wand: what changes if this were solved
- C6e: Lets silence breathe instead of rushing

### C7 Desired situation (weight 10)
- C7a: Asks them to paint the picture a year from now
- C7b: Asks why that is important to them
- C7c: Asks what part they most look forward to

### C8 Tie-down & transition (weight 5)
- C8a: Asks if there is anything else they should know
- C8b: Reflects their situation back and gets permission to walk through how Kim helps

### C9 Pitch: promise, 4 pillars, delivery (weight 15)
- C9a: High-level promise of process and visible change, no outcome guarantee
- C9b: Pillar 1, The Honest Read, tied to what they've tried
- C9c: Pillar 2, The Reset (profile, photos, messaging)
- C9d: Pillar 3, The Inner Game
- C9e: Pillar 4, Read & Lead
- C9f: Delivery: group calls twice weekly, library, community, 1:1 for paid tiers
- C9g: Checks for questions or understanding

### C10 Temperature check (weight 10)
- C10a: Asks how they feel about the process
- C10b: Uses the 1 to 10 scale when the answer is uncertain
- C10c: Handles what keeps them from 9 or 10 before price

### C11 Next steps before price (weight 5)
- C11a: Paints getting started before revealing the investment

### C12 Investment (weight 15)
- C12a: Recommends one tier based on discovery
- C12b: Ties the recommendation to what they said
- C12c: States the price and stays silent
- C12d: Does not dump all tiers

### C13 Objection pacing (weight 10)
- C13a: Takes money off the table and checks belief in the process first
- C13b: Tie-down: 'not should I, but how do I make this work'
- C13c: Does not hand out payment plans to an uncertainty objection


## Triage / setter call: Kimberly Rae Coaching: setter phone call

Score = weighted share of applicable steps (hit 1, partial 0.5, miss 0).

### S1 Open & anchor (weight 10)
- S1a: Confirms who they're speaking to and introduces self as Kimberly's team
- S1b: Anchors to what the lead did (application, quiz, training, DM)

### S2 Frame & permission (weight 10)
- S2a: Explains the purpose (point them in the right direction)
- S2b: Gets permission to ask a few questions

### S3 Discovery (weight 25)
- S3a: Biggest thing not working in dating/relationships
- S3b: Digs in: what does that look like, how long
- S3c: Relationship status / background
- S3d: What they've tried and how it went
- S3e: Doubt: what's getting in the way

### S4 Why now, cost & desire (weight 15)
- S4a: Why now
- S4b: Cost of the problem, spillover into life
- S4c: Desired picture if solved

### S5 Sell the call (weight 10)
- S5a: Reflects their situation back in one line
- S5b: Sells the consultation call (worst case clarity, best case changes it)

### S6 Financial qualification (weight 15)
- S6a: Asks if they can invest if it's the right fit
- S6b: Uses only the range anchor (low to mid four figures); no specific prices or plans
- S6c: Handles hesitation with the resourcefulness reframe or financing/credit check

### S7 Book & confirm (weight 10)
- S7a: Offers a live transfer or two specific times
- S7b: Confirms timezone and email
- S7c: Has them accept the calendar invite while on the phone

### S8 Lock the show (weight 5)
- S8a: Gets their word to reschedule rather than no-show
- S8b: Quiet place, present, not driving
- S8c: Connects them to the closer (intro text) and/or sends the pre-call video

## Output per call

```json
{"call_id": "...", "rep": "...", "score": 0, "hard_flags": [{"flag": "...", "quote": "...", "timestamp": "..."}],
```

When the temperature check returns 'I really don't know', stay there and scale it before price; never answer a value doubt with improvised $4,000 and $1,000 offers, and drop 'when we get you there... getting married' language.

Strong discovery and a clean pitch, but quoting 50%/78% relationship rates breaks the no-outcome-promise rule. Ask the doubt question and confirm she has the full call time before the pitch so the close isn't cut by her next meeting.

Discovery was thorough but meandered for 90 minutes on a low-intent, low-budget prospect; qualify budget and intent early and release cleanly instead of using faith arguments to hold someone who has said no three times.

Discovery was long and circled her readiness for 40 minutes, and she twice had to ask for the price, which she read as pressure. Get the tie-down on timing before the pitch, name tiers accurately, and do not hold price hostage once the prospect asks.

Strong discovery and a clean temperature check, but the investment section unravelled: tier one was quoted as the 6-month 14K, then a $3,400 bi-weekly price that isn't on the sheet, then a custom $500/month plan. This was a strong, well-sequenced call. Two things to fix: add the recording disclosure, and never use another client's name and personal anxiety details as a proof story.

Run the temperature check before price and stop pushing once a genuine cash-flow constraint
